title: Solve a cubic with at least one integer root

steps: Split the terms so (x - 1) can be taken out
Use the known root x = 2 to get a factor
problems.note: Same grouping method, but the root x = 2 is given, the leading coefficient is now 2, and the quadratic factor has two different roots (4.5 and 7). The slots keep the same meanings.

steps: Subtract to leave the remainder so far
Set f(x) = 0 and solve each factor
problems.note: The root x = -1 is given, and the quadratic factor 2x² - 23x + 63 is the same as in the last problem. This time you find it by long division by (x + 1) instead of grouping. The slots keep the same meanings.

title: Plot complex numbers on an Argand diagram

steps: Read off the real and imaginary parts

problems.note: Only one point this time, and its real part is negative, so you move left from the origin. Reading the parts and plotting work as before.

steps: Write each number as a point (Re, Im)
problems.note: Three numbers this time instead of one, and z₂ has a negative imaginary part. The reading and plotting steps are the same as before.

title: Add, subtract and multiply complex numbers

steps: Plot each point as (real part, imaginary part)
problems.note: This time z₂ is subtracted rather than added, so every sign inside its bracket flips. Reading the parts and combining them work as before. A last step plots the three points, which is new.
The numbers are now multiplied by 4 and 5, and both z₂ and z₃ are given, so both brackets must be expanded. The steps are the same as before.

title: Raise to a power with De Moivre's Theorem

steps: Write 1 + i in polar form and apply De Moivre's Theorem
Write in polar form and cube it
problems.note: The point is now in the second quadrant, the modulus is 1 and the power is 3, so the reference angle matters. The method is the same: modulus, then argument, then raise to the power.

steps: Evaluate and write as a + bi
problems.note: The point is now in the fourth quadrant, so the argument is negative, and the power is 9. The steps are the same as the previous problem.

title: Solve zⁿ = a (incl. nth roots of unity)

steps: Apply De Moivre's theorem for the cube root
Take the square root of v
problems.note: There are two roots this time, not three, and the number is already in polar form. The method is the same: root the modulus, halve the angle, then read off each value. The ± gives both roots instead of trying n = 0 and n = 1.

steps: Find the argument in the second quadrant
Take the square root using De Moivre
Find the first root using n = 0
Find the second root using n = 1
problems.note: This time the number is not in polar form, so you first find its modulus and argument from the point. The square root then uses 2nπ with n = 0 and n = 1, as in the first problem, rather than the ± used last time.

title: Divide complex numbers

steps: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom
Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom
Divide each part of the top by 5
problems.note: Changed from the first: the top is the real number 15 rather than a complex number, so only 15 has to be multiplied out against the conjugate. The bottom and the method (multiply by the conjugate, then divide) stay the same.

steps: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of 2 − i
Divide and write in the form a + bi
problems.note: Changed from the second: the top is a complex number again, so both brackets are expanded, and the bottom is 2 − i, so its conjugate is 2 + i (the sign of the i flips). The first step also writes the question's division w = z₁ ÷ z₂ as a fraction. The method stays the same.

title: Find the modulus as distance from the origin

steps: Use the modulus formula |a + bi| = √(a² + b²)

problems.note: Changed from the first: the number is not given directly. Subtract z₃ from z₂ first to get −9 + 5i, then use the same modulus formula.
Changed from the second: this time the root does not come out whole, so the last step writes it as a surd: 40 = 4 × 10 and √4 = 2. The modulus formula and the sum of squares stay the same.

title: Use ratio and direct/inverse proportion

steps: Find the value of one part (children’s tickets)
Find the total person-days of work
problems.note: Changed from the first: this is inverse proportion, so the total work is found first (6 × 8 person-days) and then shared by the number of people, rather than split into ratio parts. The answer is still the total divided by a number.

steps: Find the cost of one metre
problems.note: Changed from the second: this is direct proportion, so the cost goes up with the length. The total is divided to get the cost of one metre, and that is multiplied by the new length.

title: Work in scientific notation

steps: Write 165 in the form a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10
problems.note: Changed from the first: the number is given in words (165 billion), so the first step turns it into a power of ten before the number is written as a × 10ⁿ. The two slots keep the same meaning.
Changed from the second: the number is now the result of a division and a multiplication, so the a × 10ⁿ form comes at the end and a is rounded. The a and 10ⁿ colours keep the same meaning.

title: Decide whether a function is increasing or decreasing at a point

problems.note: Changed from the first: the derivative is already given, so there is no differentiating; the work is substituting into a trig function and reading its sign. The test is the same: increasing when the derivative is greater than 0.

steps: Find v'(1) and decide what it says about the slope
Find v''(1) and decide what it says about the curve
problems.note: Changed from the second: this part also uses the second derivative, to see whether the rate of increase is slowing or speeding up, which picks one graph. The substitution and the sign test are unchanged.

title: Find a point of inflection

steps: Set h''(x) = 0 to find the inflection point
problems.note: This one is a height h(x) in metres, so it is set in a real context rather than bare algebra. The steps stay the same: set the second derivative to zero, then find the height at that x.

steps: Find the point of inflection: set f''(x) = 0
problems.note: Back to bare algebra, with whole numbers rather than decimals. The method is the same, and the last step checks the point on the line g(x).

title: Solve a max/min problem from a context

steps: Set the derivative equal to zero
Check that it is a maximum
problems.note: This one is a volume V(t) rather than profit, and the derivative is again linear. The new step is checking the maximum with the second derivative: V″(t) = −6 is negative, so it is a maximum.

steps: Set the rate of change equal to 0
problems.note: The rate of change is now a quadratic, so you must factorise and reject the root outside 0 ≤ t ≤ 9. Setting the rate to zero is the same, but there is a new last step: substitute t back into the amount function to find the maximum amount.

title: Apply differentiation to rates of change

problems.note: Same amount function, now at t = 7 instead of t = 4. The answer is negative this time, so the explanation step is new.
This is the velocity of a ball, and the question asks for speed, so the minus sign is dropped at the end. The method is the same: substitute the time into the derivative.

title: Solve connected rates of change

steps: Differentiate the volume of a sphere
Use the chain rule for the rate of change of the radius
Differentiate the surface area of a sphere
Use the chain rule with the result from part (i)
problems.note: The question now asks for the rate of the surface area, not the radius, and the known rate is dr/dt from the problem before. What stays the same is the chain rule.

steps: Find the side length when V = 1/64
problems.note: The shape is now a cube and the volume is shrinking, so the known rate is negative. The side length is not given, so it is found from the volume first. The chain rule works the same way, linking the volume rate to the side length.

title: Find the slope and equation of a tangent

steps: Write the line through (1, -5) with slope 7
Rearrange into the form ax + by + c = 0
problems.note: The slope is given in the question, so there is no derivative step. The point-slope formula and the rearranging stay the same.

steps: Use the point and the slope
problems.note: The answer is now asked in the form y = mx + c, not ax + by + c = 0. The slope and point change, but the steps are otherwise the same.

title: Find and classify turning points

steps: Differentiate and set the derivative equal to zero
Set the derivative equal to zero
problems.note: The x² term is now positive, so the curve is U-shaped and the turning point is a minimum, not a maximum. Only x is asked here, so there is no y-value step. The method is the same.

steps: Set h'(x) = 0 at the greatest depth
problems.note: The function is now a depth in a real context, and its coefficients are fractions. The derivative h′(x) is given, so there is no differentiating. It is still a minimum, the lowest point, and the same steps apply.

title: Apply the chain rule

steps: Identify the outer and inner functions

problems.note: The power is now −1, so the answer needs a positive power at the end. The inside is a quadratic, 5x² + 7, but the chain rule steps are the same: outside derivative times inside derivative.
The outside function is now a cosine instead of a power, with constants in front and added on. The method is the same: outside derivative times inside derivative, then simplify the constants.

title: Differentiate exponential functions

problems.note: The exponent is now negative, −0.05t, so the quantity falls and the rate is negative. The 10⁶ factor just stays in front, and the steps are the same: differentiate, then substitute.
The exponent is now positive, 0.065t, so the colony grows instead of falling. The steps are the same: bring the rate down, then substitute the time.

title: Differentiate from first principles

problems.note: The leading term is now x², and there is a constant −10 at the end. The constant cancels when you subtract f(x), so the steps are the same.
The function is written as a squared bracket, (2x + 4)², so it must be expanded first. After that, the first-principles steps are the same as before.

title: Differentiate logarithms

steps: Differentiate the logarithm using the chain rule
Differentiate c using the chain rule
problems.note: The inside is now t², not a linear expression, so the reciprocal is 1/t² and the inside derivative is 2t. The same two parts are multiplied, then a common factor of t cancels.

steps: Interpret the sign of P'(t) in part (ii)
problems.note: The function is now P(t) = 0.82 − 0.12 ln(t+1): a constant and a coefficient in front of the log. The derivative uses the same rule, then you substitute t = 1 and interpret the sign of the answer.

title: Differentiate a polynomial by rule

problems.note: The rule is the same, but this function is a cost in t rather than bare algebra in x, and its cubic term is negative.

steps: Substitute x = 1 to find the slope
problems.note: The function is bare algebra again, with a constant 7, and the question then asks for a slope, which adds a second step.

title: Apply the product rule

steps: Name the two factors and differentiate each
Differentiate v with the chain rule
problems.note: Same product rule, but the second factor is a sine of 1/x, so v′ needs the chain rule, and the final step is in radians.

steps: Differentiate $3x\ln x$ with the product rule
problems.note: This time both factors are simple (3x and ln x), so no chain rule is needed, but the answer has two extra terms, −9 and 4/x, which are differentiated one term at a time.

title: Differentiate trig functions (radians)

problems.note: The chain rule is the same as before, but this function uses cos, has a constant 2 and a negative amplitude, so the minus signs need care.
The chain rule steps match the last problem, but the amplitude is now positive, and the question is about a tide, so the sign of the answer tells you whether it is rising or falling.

title: Calculate an average rate of change over time

steps: Find the distance from A to B
Find the time from A to B
Add the times and find the total distance
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time
problems.note: Now there are two legs of 120 km at different speeds, so you add the two times before dividing, rather than using one leg.

steps: Distance covered in the first 2 minutes
Total time for an average of 100 km/hour
Average speed over the last 6 km
Find the speed v at B
problems.note: This is a longer problem: the earlier steps find the final speed of 60 km/h. The last step uses the same idea, change in quantity divided by time, but the quantity is now the drop in speed, so the answer is a rate of change of speed.

title: Apply compound interest

steps: Find the value after each year

problems.note: Same formula with new numbers: €4500 at 2.8%. It also asks for the amount after 1 year first, which is a single multiplication, before the 3-year power.
The unknown is now the starting sum P, so the formula is solved backwards: divide by the growth factor instead of multiplying. The rate is 3% and the time is 2 years.

title: Cost materials, labour and wastage

steps: Multiply by the cost per square metre
problems.note: Same method as the tins problem: find the quantity, then multiply by the price per unit. This time the quantity is three areas added together, and no rounding up is needed.

steps: Round to the nearest ten euro
problems.note: The grass area is now found by subtracting the pond rather than adding parts. The answer is also rounded to the nearest ten euro, while the method (area times price per square metre) is the same.

title: Apply reducing-balance depreciation

problems.note: Same 20% fall, so each year leaves 0.8 of the value, but the starting value is now €30 000 and the value is needed after 1 year and after 2 years, so it is worked out year by year rather than with a power.

The rate is now 15%, so each year leaves 0.85 of the value instead of 0.8, and the value is needed after 5 years. The method is the same: find the fraction left each year, take a power of it, then multiply by the starting value.

title: Calculate percentage error, tolerance and accumulated error

steps: Divide by the intended amount and multiply by 100
Calculate and round to 2 decimal places
problems.note: This uses the same formula as the first problem, but the values are decimal areas and the actual value (31.8) goes in the denominator. The answer is rounded to 2 decimal places instead of a whole number.

steps: Write the percentage error as a decimal
problems.note: The percentage error is given and the true value is the unknown, so the formula is rearranged to find V instead of being used forwards. The rest of the method is like the first two problems.

title: Calculate income tax, USC, PRSI and net pay

steps: Add the income tax and the health insurance
Write the deductions as a percentage of her gross wage
problems.note: Same idea as the net pay problem, but there are three deductions to add (tax, USC and PRSI) and the answer is also written as a percentage of the gross wage. Both answers come from the same total.

steps: Set the tax credit equal to the tax at 20%
problems.note: The unknown is now the income rather than the tax, so the tax is set equal to the credit and solved as an equation instead of being added up. The only percentage used is the 20% rate.

title: Find the repayment on a loan/mortgage

steps: Write the repayment formula and its values
Evaluate the power and then the fraction

problems.note: The rate is given as a percentage, so it must be changed to a decimal (0.00287) first. The term is 25 years, so there are 300 monthly payments; the formula itself is the same as the first problem.

steps: Substitute P = 5000, i = 0.00157 and t = 156 into the formula
problems.note: The yearly rate is spread over 52 weeks, so the weekly rate has to be worked out from (1 + i)⁵² = 1.085 before the formula can be used. The formula and substitution are otherwise the same as the first problem.

title: Calculate percentages and percentage change

problems.note: Changed from finding a percentage of an amount to adding a percentage to it. The bill goes up by 13.5%, so the multiplier is 1.135 and the answer is the new total; the original amount stays in slot 2 and the answer in slot 3.

steps: Leave votes as a fraction of valid votes
problems.note: Changed from finding an amount to finding what percentage one number is of another. The part goes in slot 1, the whole in slot 2, and the percentage is the answer in slot 3, as before.

title: Calculate cost/selling price, discount, mark-up and margin

steps: Find the multiplier for a 25% profit
Find the margin as a percentage of the selling price
Mark up is profit as a percentage of cost price
problems.note: Changed from working forwards from a cost to working backwards from a margin given on the selling price. So a selling price of 100 is picked first, and the mark-up is profit over cost, not over selling price.
This one is mostly algebra with no numbers: 10% off means multiplying by 0.9, and r is a fixed amount taken off. You write each price in terms of p, subtract, then simplify.

title: Convert between annual and periodic rates (AER/APR)

steps: Set up the equivalent monthly rate
Set the quarterly growth factor so that 4 quarters match one year
Take the fourth root and solve for i
problems.note: Changed from monthly to quarterly: four quarters make a year, so the root is the fourth root instead of the twelfth. The annual factor stays in slot 1 and the answer as a percentage in slot 3.

steps: Convert the increase to a percentage
problems.note: Changed from a fixed number of periods to continuous growth: the factor over one year is e to the 0.04, with no root, and the answer is the annual effective rate. The factor stays in slot 1 and the answer in slot 3.

title: Find the rate or time in a compound interest problem

steps: Write the growth factor for 3 years
Take the cube root of both sides
Take the cube root of both sides
Subtract 1 and convert to a percentage
problems.note: Changed from being given the growth factor to being given the start and end amounts, so the factor has to be worked out by dividing first. The rate stays in slot 2 and the answer as a percentage in slot 3.

Changed from Problem 2: 4 years instead of 3, so you take the fourth root, and the rate sits in the formula as r/100 (a percentage) rather than as a decimal. The steps are the same: divide, take the root, subtract 1.

title: Change units (metric, imperial with factors, currency)

steps: Multiply the euro amount by the rate
Divide the pounds by the euros
problems.note: Changed from multiplying by a given rate to finding the rate by dividing one pair of amounts. The answer is now the rate itself, which stays in slot 2.

steps: Divide to find the length of 1 nautical mile
problems.note: Changed from a currency to a unit of distance, with the rate given as 27 nautical miles equal to 50 km. The steps are the same: divide, then give the converted amount in slot 3.

title: Interpret f(x) = g(x) as a comparison of functions

steps: Find where the two graphs cross
Find where k(x) is less than m(x)

problems.note: Changed from Problem 1: instead of finding where the graphs cross, this asks you to compare the two values at one x-value. Both functions are still given as bare formulas.
Changed from Problem 2: the same one-value comparison, but now in context. The two rules are charges for hours, so you read or calculate both charges and compare them.

title: Evaluate a function

problems.note: Changed from Problem 1: the input is now t = 0 instead of 2.4. The rule and the steps stay the same.
Changed from Problem 2: the rule is now f(t) = −4t² + 16t + 1 for a ball hit at t = 0, instead of h(t). The input and the steps stay the same.

title: Graph a cubic function

steps: Plot the points and join them with a smooth curve
Plot the points and join them
problems.note: Changed from Problem 1: the coefficients are now decimals (0.001, −0.12 and 3.6), so each term needs more careful arithmetic. The method is the same: substitute, then plot the points and join them with a smooth curve.

steps: Plot the ten points from the table
Join the points with a smooth curve
problems.note: Changed from Problem 2: there is no formula. The ten points are already in a table of hours and units, so you plot them rather than working them out. The method is the same: plot the points, then join them with a smooth curve.

title: Graph an exponential function

steps: Use the value given for D(2)
Use the value given for D(6)
Plot the points and draw the curve
problems.note: Changed from Problem 1: the numbers are bigger (a starting value of 2100 and a factor of 1.18), and the table runs from t = 0 to 6. The method is the same: substitute, then plot the points and join them.

steps: Plot the points from the table
Join each set with a smooth curve and label
problems.note: Changed from Problem 2: no formula is given. The points for two exponential curves, f and g, are already in a table (one x-value is ln 4, about 1.39). You still plot the points and join each set with a smooth curve.

title: Graph a linear function

steps: Find two points on the line

problems.note: Changed from Problem 1: the rule is now p(x) = 1.5x with no constant term, so the line passes through the origin. You still need two points, and the solution uses x = 40 and x = 70.

steps: Find the end points of the slope 2 segment
Find the end points of the slope $-\tfrac{2}{3}$ segment
problems.note: Changed from Problem 2: the line is drawn only between two limits, so you first work out where it stops. The slope and the two-point method stay the same.

title: Graph a quadratic function

steps: Mark the points from parts (a) and (b)
Draw the curve through the three points
Plot the points from the table
Join the points with a smooth curve
problems.note: Instead of roots and a turning point given, you now plot seven points from a table and join them. The downward shape from the negative x² term is the same idea.

steps: Plot the points from the table
problems.note: The table is now a profit function with much larger values, so the question is about profit. The plotting and joining steps are the same as before.

title: Solve equations approximately from graphs

steps: Find where the curve meets the t-axis

problems.note: Changed from Problem 1: you start from a given time and read the height, instead of finding the time where the height is 0. The method is the same: follow the curve and read the other axis.

steps: Find where the two graphs cross
problems.note: Now the target is the graph of B rather than a fixed value, so the answer is the point where the two graphs cross. You still read the x-value (h) from that point, as before.

title: Transform a graph

steps: Find the translation that maps A onto C
Apply the translation to the maximum point (2.177, 4.529)
problems.note: The shift is now worked out from two points, A and C, with decimals, instead of being given in the question. Applying it to a point works as in the previous problem.

steps: Work out the formula for g(x)
Shift the graph of f two units to the right
problems.note: The change is that the transformation is now a formula in x − 2, so you expand it first and then move each point of f two units right. Plotting and labelling the new graph are the same as before.

title: Prove triangles congruent (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS)

steps: Find three pairs of equal sides
Pick out the matching parts of the two triangles
problems.note: The triangles are now right-angled, so the test changes from three sides to RHS: a right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side. Picking out the equal parts and naming the test are the same steps as before.

steps: Match the first pair of sides
Match the angle between those sides
Match the second pair of sides
problems.note: The triangles are no longer right-angled, and the test is now SAS: two sides and the angle between them, all from the parallelogram's opposite sides and angles. Matching the parts and naming the test are the same steps as before.

title: Apply Corollary 3: An angle in a semicircle is a right angle

steps: Use the angle in a semicircle
Use the angle in a semicircle
Use angles standing on the same arc
Angles in triangle ADC add to 180 degrees
problems.note: The right angle from the semicircle is only the first step: it sets up an isosceles triangle, then equal angles on the same arc, then the angle sum finds ∠ADC. In the previous problem the right angle was the answer.

steps: (i) Explain why the angle CBD is 90 degrees
(ii) Find the first pair of equal angles
Find the second pair of equal angles
Find the third pair and conclude
problems.note: The diameter is not stated, so you must find it from the symmetry of the diagram before citing Corollary 3. The second half then aims at similar triangles rather than an angle.

title: Construct and analyse an enlargement

steps: Multiply the area by the scale factor squared
Areas change by the scale factor squared
problems.note: This time the image area is given and the original area is the unknown, so you divide by k² instead of multiplying. The rule that areas scale by k² stays the same.

steps: Multiply the side by the scale factor
problems.note: This asks for a length, not an area, so the scale factor is used once instead of squared. Multiplying the original by k works the same way as before.

title: Find the centre and scale factor of an enlargement

steps: Join each vertex to its image

problems.note: The centre is already marked, so this time you measure from it and calculate k instead of constructing the centre. The ratio stays image distance over original distance.

steps: Find the distance from the centre to Q'
Divide the image distance by the original distance
problems.note: This time the image distance is not measured: it is found by adding the given extra length 4 to |XQ|. The ratio of image over original distance is unchanged.

title: Find lengths using similar triangles

steps: Divide the bigger side by the smaller side
Multiply the shortest side by the scale factor
problems.note: This time the scale factor is not given: you find it first from two lengths (45 and 36), then multiply a third length by it. The idea that matching sides share one ratio is unchanged.

steps: Find the height x of the removed top cone
problems.note: This is a real context, two similar cones, and the answer needs one subtraction after the ratio step. The ratio idea is the same as the last problem.

title: Apply Theorem 14: Pythagoras

steps: Set up Pythagoras on half of the roof triangle
problems.note: This time the two shorter sides are not given: you work them out from the roof measurements first, then use the same Pythagoras method.

steps: Take the square root and round
problems.note: The unknown is now a shorter side, not the hypotenuse, so the known squares are subtracted. Pythagoras itself is unchanged.

title: Apply Theorem 2: Isosceles triangle: equal sides ⇔ equal base angles

steps: Find the angle DOB on the straight line
Find the base angle of triangle OBC
Double it to get the angle of the pentagon
problems.note: This time the apex angle is given and the base angle is only a step: the answer is twice it. The isosceles rule is the same as before.
This chains two isosceles triangles with a straight-line step between them. The base-angle rule is the same as before, but it is needed twice.

title: Apply Theorem 20: Tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact (and converse)

steps: Use Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle ATB
Find the angle at A in triangle AOD
problems.note: This time the unknown is an angle, not a length. The tangent only comes in at the last step, but it still gives the 90° at the point of contact that you need.

steps: Use the radius as the height of triangle HSP
problems.note: Now the answer is an area in terms of r, not a number. The radius is still the height, and the 90° at the point of contact is still what makes it the height.

title: Apply Theorem 4: Angles in a triangle sum to 180°

steps: Use the angles in triangle ABC
Use the angles of a triangle
problems.note: The two unknown angles are now written in terms of A, so you set up an equation and solve for A. The angle-sum rule is the same as problem 1, and the right angle is the known angle.

steps: Find the angle inside the bottom triangle at line k
problems.note: Now there are several triangles, and each angle you find is used in the next triangle. The 180° rule is the same as before, applied again and again.

title: Apply Theorem 9: Parallelogram: opposite sides and opposite angles equal

steps: Opposite angles are equal: find x
Substitute x = 65 and solve for y
problems.note: The angles are now expressions in x and y, so each rule gives an equation and you solve them one after the other. The two rules are the same as in problem 1.

steps: Use the opposite sides of the parallelogram
problems.note: There is no angle now. The parallelogram sits on a grid, and you find a missing corner with the same rule: opposite sides are equal and parallel, so [TQ] is a copy of [FB].

title: Find images under translation, central symmetry, axial symmetry and rotation

steps: Find the translation that takes U to V
Apply the same translation to Q
Find the translation that takes S to P
Apply the same translation to R
problems.note: The move now comes from a square. Since PQRS is a square, S to P is the same move as R to Q, so you find the move from S and P and apply it to R. The method is the same as problem 1.

steps: Find L using the symmetry about the y-axis
problems.note: The move is now a reflection in the y-axis, not a translation: the y-value stays the same and the x-value changes sign. The length and the line are then found from L and M.

title: Construction 21: Centroid of a triangle

steps: Draw two medians and mark the centroid
problems.note: Same compass method as problem 1, on a new triangle PQR. There are two midpoints to find, M1 on PQ and M2 on QR, and the medians run from R and from P.
Same centroid method, but the midpoints come from measured lengths, not compass arcs. Measure each side, halve it and mark it. The rest of the steps are unchanged.

title: Solve an exponential equation reducible to a quadratic

steps: Set each factor equal to zero
Take natural logs to solve for k
Set f(x) equal to g(x) and clear the fraction
Treat it as a quadratic in e^x
Reject the impossible value and solve for x
problems.note: This time the equation has a fraction with $e^x$ on the bottom, so you clear it first, and one root is impossible and is rejected. The substitution and taking ln are the same as before.

steps: Write the equation in the form of part (i)
Take log base 3 of both sides
Split the log into the form log_3 p - q
problems.note: This time the base is 3, so $3^{2m+1}$ is first rewritten as $3(3^m)^2$ and you take log base 3 at the end. The substitution and the rejected root are the same as before.

title: Solve an exponential equation with a common base

steps: Write both sides as powers of 2
Write both sides of the equation with base 2 (part (ii))
problems.note: The right side is 128, which is not a power of 2 you know straight away, so you list powers of 2 to find 128 = 2⁷. The method is the same after that, and the answer comes out as a decimal.
